channel.title: AlphaPhoenix
channel.description: I'm Brian Haidet - PhD in Materials Science, but I'd also describe myself as artist, maker, and Hawaiian shirt enthusiast. On this channel, You'll find my side projects and favorite physics demos - I hope you enjoy!

videos.t: Magnetic Levitator
videos.desc: How a photogate-based magnetic levitator works and how to build one!  I started this project during the spring semester and just got it all working.

videos.t: Dalek Door
videos.desc:
When you come visit my dorm room, beware that the dalek poster on the door isn't just a poster...  
This is an entertaining project that makes a door blink back at whoever just knocked on it through the peephole, using exclusively discrete components - no microcontroller necessary!

videos.desc: Everybody hates printers! Watch one get satisfyingly decimated by a pound of thermite!

videos.t: Doggie Doorbell
videos.desc:

videos.t: Random Box Preview
videos.desc: I'm working on a random number generator based on background radiation (True quantum-random numbers). This is the circuit working for the first time. Radiation is passing through a Geiger-Muller tube, stopping a counter and displaying the result on a Nixie Tube.

videos.t: Doggie Doorbell (circuit)

videos.t: Examining The Thermite Reaction Front
videos.desc:
I experiment with thermite to determine the rate of reaction. Thermite powder is burned in a pyrex tube and filmed from the side, so the reaction front can be seen moving through the powder. I was amazed at how slow the reaction progressed - It's extremely dependent on the container. Based on the results I observed, I would expect the fastest achievable reaction would be loosely-packed powder in a large and low-aspect-ratio thermally insulating vessel like a flowerpot.

videos.t: RainPi - Calculating Pi with Raindrops! (Part 2: How it Works)
videos.desc:
Calculating Pi with the Monte Carlo Method is a common introductory programming exercise, but I wanted to get away from computer-generated "random" numbers and used falling raindrops! The apparatus can only complete one calculation - it calculates pi with the shape of its raindrop-detecting sensors.

This Pt. 2 video explains the Monte Carlo Method, the physical construction of the rain sensor, and the program running on the Arduino to count drops.

videos.t: Star-Stabilization: The Infinite Polaris Timelapse (4k)
videos.desc:
The stars in the sky appear to move in arcs overhead, but it's actually the Earth that is spinning. They look like they're doing loops around Polaris, the north star, because it lies on the axis of Earth's rotation. If you point a camera at Polaris and spin it at the same rate as the sky turns (in the opposite direction), you can halt the rotation of the stars!

videos.t: Star-tracking camera mount: Why it works and how to build one
videos.desc:
In this video, I explain (using a bunch of timelapses) why "polar tracker" or "star tracker" camera mounts allow you to take long exposures of the sky without streaking. I also show off my polar tracking rig, which is my most recent piece of homebuilt photography equiment. It uses a door hinge and a curved lead screw to slowly rotate the camera (approximately 0.25 degrees per minute) and eliminate streaking in astrophotogrphy images.

Based on the design by Gary Seronik:
http://garyseronik.com/build-a-hinge-tracker-for-astrophotography/

It passed within about 4.9 million miles, or about 20x the Earth-moon distance. It was moving so fast across the sky you could literally watch it move over the course of a few minutes. videos.t: Measuring the speed of light the old fashioned way: Replicating the Fizeau Apparatus
videos.desc: In 1849, the first terrestrial measurement of the seed of light was made by Hippolyte Fizeau using a bright focused lamp, a spinning slotted wheel, and a reflector a few kilometers away. This famous experiment is one that I've spent the better part of the last year thinking about and very slowly replicating! Using a 5mW green-dot laser sight, a "slotted disk" laser-cut from black posterboard, a speed-controlled dremel, a digital camera, and a full spool of retroreflective tape, I succeeded in measuring and calculating the speed of light! The electric current very efficiently solves the maze, which is awesome, and heats up the "solution" so we can see it!

videos.t: Slomo of my resonance machine #physics #slowmo
videos.desc:
Somme awesome slomo shots of my home-built resonance machine! With a magnet, coil, and a bunch of slightly elastic cord, this machine can pump out whatever waves you feed it from a signal generator. 
One of the most surprising things to me was to watch how a standing wave formed - if you watch in slow motion, the standing wave is actually the sum of the original traveling wave moving right, and the reflected traveling wave moving left. they cancel each other out in perfect time to create the standing wave!

videos.t: Flying playing cards are awesome

Today I get to show off the results of my most recent high-speed filming obsession. I wanted to understand the airflow around a flying playing card - when you flick or throw a card across a room like a frisbee. Now in glorious 1500-7500ish fps video, we get wingtip effects, oscillatory vortex shedding, and gyroscopic effects. I hope you enjoy, cause I certainly had fun filming it!

videos.t: I weighed an airplane... while it was flying!
videos.desc:
Theoretically, it should be possible to measure the weight of a flying object from far below that object - by measuring the air that object displaced when it pushes on the ground.  I HAD to know if this was realistically possible, so I set about building a very large scale to measure paper airplanes and flying playing cards. After getting successful measurements, I decided to go full scale with real airplanes.

videos.t: I DROPPED my slomo camera to explain how gravity works
videos.desc:
Today we're talking about gravity! From classical Newtonian gravity to General Relativity, I want to explain a key bit of physics called the equivalence principle: Why gravitational mass and inertial mass have the same value, or said differently, why heavy things are hard to push. The primary trick here is that general relativity allows us to predict "where to put the camera" to define an inertial reference frame. Unfortunately for my sanity, "where to put the camera" is "in freefall", and I'm using my very nice highspeed camera… Hope you enjoy!

Huge thanks to Dr. Ortega from Universidad de Z

videos.t: Slow-motion frogs are goofier than I expected
videos.desc:
More backyard slomo critters that have nerd-sniped me! Today we're looking at tree frogs on glass - how they stick, when they don't, when they catch moths, and… when they don't. Turns out these frogs are not graceful hunters when slowed down 50x, but they're still awesome. The physics behind their phenomenal adhesion is very unique, and the biology of their prey-tracking behavior is very unexpected. I learned a lot by watching these guys for weeks while they collected moths on my back patio door, and I thoroughly enjoyed recording their antics in slomo. I hope you enjoy too!
